entities.name: Albert Decourtray
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Albert Decourtray (1923–1994) was a French cardinal and Archbishop of Lyon, one of the most significant Catholic voices in France during the 1980s and early 1990s. Born in Lille, he was ordained a priest and consecrated bishop before being appointed Archbishop of Lyon in 1981 and elevated to cardinal in 1985. Lyon—the oldest and historically most important see in Gaul—gave him a platform of exceptional prestige.

Decourtray became a prominent public intellectual and moral voice in French society during a period of intense debate about immigration, the National Front's rise, religious pluralism, and the legacy of Vichy. He was a vigorous opponent of racism and the extreme right, engaging publicly with the challenge of integrating Muslim immigrants into French society while insisting on the nation's Catholic civilisational heritage. His pastoral letters on these subjects attracted national attention.

He was also involved in the complex question of the Carmelite convent at Auschwitz, which created intense friction between Jewish groups and the Catholic Church. He worked to mediate this controversy with sensitivity to both the Church's need to honour its own martyrs and the Jewish community's insistence on Auschwitz's unique character as the primary site of Holocaust memory. He died of cancer in 1994 before fully completing this work.
